name: Classical Nahuatl
variety: Classical Nahuatl of the Valley of Mexico in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, as reconstructed from colonial grammars (above all Carochi 1645) and modern philology; there are no recordings, so all phonetic detail is reconstructed
sources: Carochi, Horacio (1645). Arte de la lengua mexicana con la declaración de los adverbios della. México.
Andrews, J. Richard (2003). Introduction to Classical Nahuatl, revised edition. Norman: University of Oklahoma Press.
Launey, Michel (2011). An Introduction to Classical Nahuatl, translated and adapted by Christopher Mackay. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
Karttunen, Frances (1983). An Analytical Dictionary of Nahuatl. Austin: University of Texas Press.
Lockhart, James (2001). Nahuatl as Written. Stanford: Stanford University Press.
contrasts: short versus long vowels in four qualities: toca 'to follow' versus tōca 'to bury', tlatia 'to burn' versus tlātia 'to hide'
glottal stop (saltillo) after a vowel versus its absence; it also marks the plural of many nouns and verbs
lateral affricate tɬ versus t and l
labialised velar kʷ versus k, also at the end of a syllable (tēuctli with /kʷ/)
three affricates ts, tʃ, tɬ and two sibilants s, ʃ
no voiced stops, no r; four vowel qualities without a separate u
allophony: /w/ is voiceless [ʍ] at the end of a syllable (written uh)
/l/ is voiceless at the end of a syllable; /j/ does not occur there, where it is replaced by [ʃ]
/n/ takes the place of a following consonant, is weak or velar at the end of a word and is often left unwritten there
/m/ becomes n at the end of a word and before consonants other than labials
/tɬ/ becomes l after l: cal plus tli gives calli, with a long [lː]
/kʷ/ keeps its rounding at the end of a syllable as a voiceless release (written uc or cuh)
/o/ varies between [o] and [u]; colonial texts write both o and u
the glottal stop occurs only after a vowel; at the end of an utterance it is reported as a stronger, breath-like sound, and other dialects have [h] throughout
long vowels are shortened before a glottal stop and at the end of a word before a pause
syllable_structure: (C)V(C), with a short or long vowel; no clusters inside a syllable
phonotactics: at most two consonants meet, across a syllable boundary in the middle of a word
words do not begin or end with a cluster; the noun ending is -tl after a vowel, -tli after a consonant and -li after l
a supporting vowel i is inserted where a cluster would arise
geminates arise at morpheme boundaries and are written double (calli, mitzittac)

stress.rule: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word; the only exception is the vocative ending -é used by men, which is stressed.
stress.cues: not recoverable for the classical language; in modern Nahuatl varieties pitch and duration

rhythm.notes: Rhythm cannot be observed for an extinct stage of the language; class and final lengthening are neutral defaults, not findings. Contrastive vowel length and closed syllables make syllable weight relevant to timing.

length.notes: Vowel length is contrastive and is written with a macron only in modern editions; colonial texts, except Carochi and a few others, leave it unmarked. The ratio of long to short vowels is unknown. Long consonants arise only at morpheme boundaries, above all ll.

intonation.declarative: not recoverable; the colonial grammars do not describe sentence melody
intonation.yes_no_question: marked by the particle cuix; melody not recoverable
intonation.wh_question: question words (āc, tleh, cān, īc) begin the clause; melody not recoverable
intonation.notes: The pitch range value is a neutral default.

tone.notes: Carochi's accent marks note vowel length and the glottal stop, not tone.

phonation: voiceless sonorants at the end of a syllable

problems: tl is the sequence t plus voiced l; there is no voiceless lateral affricate [tɬ]
kʷ at the end of a syllable is wrong: uc is read as [wk] (tēuctli comes out as [teːwktli]) and cuh as [kw] plus a glottal stop
vowel length depends on macrons in the text; the usual unmarked spelling gives short vowels everywhere
w at the end of a syllable (uh) is a voiced [w]; l, n are not devoiced or weakened there
long vowels are not shortened before the glottal stop or at the end of a word
no separate handling of the glottal stop at the end of an utterance
good: penultimate stress, with final stress for the vocative ē
the saltillo written h is a glottal stop
macron vowels are long; ll is a long l
spelling rules for c, qu, cu, hu, z, x, tz, ch

notes: No acoustic data exist for Classical Nahuatl. Values from modern Nahuatl varieties should not be copied into this profile without saying so.
